query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small dispersion of ZrC into the boride matrix will improve the resistance of boride-based components to molten aluminum corrosion by creating localized inert barriers that limit aluminum dissolution.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional boride-based component used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, composed solely of the boride phase.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a low volume fraction (e.g., <5 wt.%) of fine ZrC particles into the boride matrix via an appropriate processing method (e.g., powder metallurgy or surface modification).
generation.conditions: The component is exposed to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (approximately 660°C) under standard processing durations.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform dispersion of fine ZrC particles that form localized barrier phases at grain boundaries or within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Refractory and chemically inert ZrC particles act as corrosion-resistant barriers that reduce the effective contact area between the boride and the aggressive molten aluminum, thereby slowing the dissolution process and improving overall corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components with the ZrC dispersion will exhibit a significantly lower corrosion rate (as measured by lower weight loss and reduced degradation) compared to untreated, pure boride components under identical molten aluminum exposure conditions.
generation.baseline: Pure boride-based components without any ZrC addition subjected to the same molten aluminum plating conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only if the ZrC remains uniformly dispersed and adherent in the boride matrix at the operating temperature; excessive doping or agglomeration of ZrC could negatively affect mechanical integrity.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the corrosion rate reduction is uncertain and may depend on the quality of the ZrC dispersion and the interfacial integrity between ZrC and boride; further optimization and systematic testing are necessary.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of boride-based components: one set with a low volume fraction (<5 wt.%) of uniformly dispersed ZrC and one set without ZrC. Subject both sets to immersion in molten aluminum at ~660°C for an identical duration. Post-exposure, conduct weight loss measurements, surface morphological analysis, and phase identification.
measurements: Weight loss measurement (to assess corrosion rate)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ZrC-dispersed components do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate or improved microstructural integrity compared to the control group, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ZrC can effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating, and the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating increases with increasing ZrC content. The annual corrosion rate of the 04ZrC coating in a 1 mol/L NaCl solution is only 21.5% of that of the HEA. Consequently, the addition of ZrC to the FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy alloy coating holds promise for applications in corrosion resistance, particularly in oceanic environments.
